1: Hannah is childless and mocked. She weeps and prays at Shiloh, promising to give her son to God. Samuel is born, and she brings him to the priest Eli.
God hears the prayer of the humiliated. Hannah gives back what she most wanted.
2: Hannah sings that God brings down the proud and lifts the lowly. Eli's sons abuse their priesthood, and a prophet announces judgement on his house.
Mary's Magnificat echoes Hannah's song. Sacred office does not excuse sin.
3: God calls the boy Samuel by name in the night. Three times he runs to Eli. Then he answers, "Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening."
Samuel's answer is a model prayer for anyone seeking God's will.
4: Israel carries the ark into battle like a lucky charm. The Philistines capture it and kill Eli's sons. Eli falls and dies at the news.
God cannot be used as a tool.
5: The ark is placed in the temple of Dagon, whose statue falls on its face before it. Plague strikes each city that holds the ark.
The Lord needs no army to defend his honour.
6: The Philistines send the ark home on a cart pulled by two cows, with gold offerings. It arrives at Beth-shemesh.
Even Israel's enemies learn to fear the Lord.
7: Israel puts away its idols and repents at Mizpah. God thunders against the Philistines. Samuel sets up a stone called Ebenezer, "stone of help".
"Thus far the Lord has helped us."
8: The elders ask for a king like other nations. God tells Samuel, "They have not rejected you; they have rejected me." Samuel warns what a king will take from them.
Wanting to be like everyone else can mean rejecting God's rule.
9: Saul, a tall young man from Benjamin, goes looking for lost donkeys and ends up at Samuel's door. God has told Samuel he is the one.
10: Samuel anoints Saul privately, and God gives him a new heart. When he is chosen publicly by lot, he is found hiding among the baggage.
Saul begins with humility. The test will be whether it lasts.
11: The Ammonites threaten Jabesh. The Spirit comes on Saul, he rallies Israel and rescues the town. He refuses to punish those who doubted him.
At his best Saul gives God the credit.
12: Samuel defends his honesty, reviews God's faithfulness and warns king and people to serve the Lord. He promises to keep praying for them.
"Far be it from me that I should sin against the Lord by ceasing to pray for you."
13: With his army melting away, Saul will not wait for Samuel and offers the sacrifice himself. Samuel tells him his kingdom will not last.
Fear leads Saul to disobey. God seeks a man after his own heart.
14: Jonathan and his armour-bearer attack a Philistine post, trusting that God can save by many or by few. Saul's rash oath nearly costs Jonathan his life.
Jonathan's faith contrasts with his father's anxious control.
15: Told to destroy Amalek completely, Saul keeps the best animals and spares the king, then blames the people. Samuel says, "To obey is better than sacrifice."
Partial obedience with a religious excuse is still disobedience.
16: God sends Samuel to Jesse's sons in Bethlehem. Seven are passed over; the youngest, David, a shepherd, is anointed. He enters Saul's service as a harpist.
"Man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart."
17: The giant Goliath taunts Israel for forty days. David, armed with a sling and five stones, says, "I come in the name of the Lord," and kills him.
Trust in God makes a shepherd boy braver than an army.
18: Jonathan loves David as his own soul. The women sing that David has killed more than Saul, and Saul's envy grows. He twice throws a spear at him.
Envy poisons Saul. Jonathan's friendship is free of it.
19: Saul orders David killed. Jonathan pleads for him, and David's wife Michal lowers him from a window.
God protects David through people who love him.
20: Jonathan tests his father's mood and warns David with a signal of arrows. The two friends weep and part.
True friendship puts the other's good first. Jonathan gives up a throne.
21: At Nob the priest gives hungry David the holy bread and Goliath's sword. In Gath David pretends to be mad to escape.
Jesus cites the holy bread to show that mercy outranks ritual rules.
22: David gathers four hundred men in distress at the cave of Adullam. Saul has eighty-five priests killed for helping him.
Saul's fear has turned into tyranny.
23: David rescues the town of Keilah and keeps asking God what to do. Saul hunts him, and Jonathan comes to strengthen him.
David seeks guidance at every step.
24: Saul enters the very cave where David is hiding. David cuts off a corner of his cloak but will not harm "the Lord's anointed".
David refuses to seize by violence what God has promised him.
25: Samuel dies. Rich, foolish Nabal insults David, who sets out for revenge. Nabal's wife Abigail hurries to meet him with gifts and wise words.
A wise word at the right time prevents bloodshed.
26: David slips into Saul's camp at night and takes his spear and water jug, leaving him unharmed.
Mercy toward an enemy, twice over.
27: Worn out, David takes refuge with the Philistine king of Gath and is given the town of Ziklag.
Even David has seasons of discouragement and compromise.
28: God no longer answers Saul. In disguise he consults a medium at Endor, which he himself had banned. Samuel appears and foretells his death.
Saul ends where disobedience leads: seeking in darkness what he refused in the light.
29: The Philistine commanders do not trust David and send him away before the battle against Israel.
God spares David from fighting his own people.
30: Raiders burn Ziklag and carry off the families. David strengthens himself in the Lord, pursues, and recovers everything. He shares the plunder with those who stayed behind.
In crisis David turns to God first.
31: The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa. Jonathan is killed, and wounded Saul falls on his own sword.
A reign that began with promise ends in tragedy.
